data.title: Pityriasis versicolor — viva
data.summary: Fungal infections · 10 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Pityriasis versicolor** (Fungal infections)_

**Q1. What is pityriasis versicolor? Agent?**
- Chronic, recurrent, superficial infection of stratum corneum by Malassezia (lipophilic yeast, normal skin flora) in its mycelial phase — mostly M. globosa, also M. furfur, M. sympodialis
- Not contagious; endogenous overgrowth

**Q2. Predisposing factors?**
- Hot humid climate, sweating, oily skin, adolescents and young adults (high sebum), oily applications, occlusion, malnutrition, steroids, immunosuppression, pregnancy, genetic predisposition

**Q3. Clinical features.**
- Multiple round/oval scaly macules coalescing into patches on upper trunk, neck, upper arms, face (children); minimal itch
- Colour: hypopigmented (most common in Indian skin), hyperpigmented (fawn/brown), erythematous — hence 'versicolor'
- Evoked scale sign (Besnier's sign) — stretching or scratching produces fine branny scale

**Q4. Why are lesions hypopigmented?**
- Azelaic acid and other dicarboxylic acids from Malassezia inhibit tyrosinase; pityriacitrin screens UV; damage to melanocytes and smaller melanosomes; persists for weeks after cure

**Q5. Why hyperpigmented in some?**
- Larger melanosomes and thicker keratin layer with inflammatory infiltrate

**Q6. Investigations.**
- KOH mount: short hyphae and round spores — 'spaghetti and meatballs'
- Wood's lamp: yellow-gold fluorescence (not always)
- Scotch tape test with methylene blue/Parker ink; culture needs olive oil-supplemented media (rarely needed)

**Q7. Differential diagnosis.**
- Hypopigmented: pityriasis alba, vitiligo (depigmented, no scale), indeterminate leprosy (sensation), post-inflammatory hypopigmentation, progressive macular hypomelanosis (no scale, red fluorescence of follicles), nevus depigmentosus, seborrhoeic dermatitis
- Hyperpigmented/red: pityriasis rosea, tinea corporis, seborrhoeic dermatitis, erythrasma, confluent and reticulated papillomatosis, secondary syphilis, café-au-lait

**Q8. Treatment.**
- Topical: ketoconazole 2% shampoo/lotion applied for 5–10 min daily for 3–5 days; selenium sulphide 2.5%; azole creams; terbinafine cream; zinc pyrithione; 20% sodium hyposulphite
- Oral for extensive or recurrent: itraconazole 200 mg/day for 5–7 days, fluconazole 300 mg weekly for 2 weeks (or 400 mg single dose); oral terbinafine is not effective; griseofulvin not effective
- Counsel that pigment takes months to normalise — not treatment failure

**Q9. Prophylaxis for recurrence?**
- Ketoconazole/selenium shampoo once or twice monthly or weekly in summer; or itraconazole 400 mg once a month during humid months

**Q10. Other Malassezia-related diseases?**
- Seborrhoeic dermatitis, Malassezia (Pityrosporum) folliculitis, confluent and reticulated papillomatosis (debated), atopic head-and-neck dermatitis, catheter-related fungaemia in neonates on lipid infusions

## Quick spotter facts
- Spaghetti and meatballs on KOH
- Evoked scale (Besnier's) sign
- Oral terbinafine doesn't work in PV

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Superficial fungal infections — Malassezia). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
